name: ancient
why: Decompression routines for long-dead file formats, a fascinating way into old binary formats and their quirks.

brief.what_it_is: Ancient is a C++ library and command-line tool that decompresses data made by old compression formats, mostly from Amiga and Atari machines in the 1980s and 1990s, plus some newer formats used in those systems. You feed it a compressed file and it detects the format in most cases and writes out the decompressed data. The README lists dozens of formats, including ByteKiller, Pack-Ice, PowerPacker, StoneCracker, DMS, XPK wrappers, and Unix compress/pack, along with gzip and bzip2. It also includes decompressor backends for Zip and LZH that are not built in yet, and it does not handle archives or self-extracting executables.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says most of these algorithms can still be downloaded, but the original implementations were written only for the machines they ran on, and some ports are incomplete, poor quality, or direct translations of M68K assembly. The project aims to provide clean modern implementations, a BSD-style license in place of unclear or missing licenses, and testing against a cache of about 10k files that used these formats.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives little detail on internals. It says the compression format is detected automatically in most cases, with some corner cases where detection is unreliable because of weaknesses in the old formats. It says the tests use a cache of roughly 10k real files plus a small batch of generated test files drawn from public domain sources. Several decompressors were re-implemented using reference code (Harri Hirvola's HA for SASC/SHSC, Lhasa for some LZH variants), and the README says no code was reused from them.
brief.install_notes: The README has no installation or build instructions. It says the code should compile cleanly on most C++17 compilers and is tested on clang and MSVC. It describes two entry points: a simple command-line application (see main.cpp) and a simple API (see api/ancient/ancient.hpp). No commands are shown in the README. Some formats have weak password protection that the code can bypass, for DMS and PowerPacker PX20. The project says it does not do real cryptography.
brief.standout: It is a single decompressor covering a large number of obscure Amiga and Atari formats, many of which exist nowhere else as clean modern code, and it is tested against thousands of real files. The author also cleared up licensing: many of the original implementations have unclear or missing licenses, and some ports are of doubtful legality, so this project rewrites them under BSD-style terms.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release date, changelog, or last-commit information. It says the author is 'slowly adding new stuff' and invites requests for new formats, which suggests the project is still being worked on, but I did not check the commit history or releases page.
brief.caveats: The README says detection is not fully reliable for some formats because of weaknesses in the old formats. Several formats are marked 'verification missing': PP 1.1, FLT!, Dupa, and PARA. Archive files and self-extracting executables are not supported. Zip and LZH decompressors exist only as backends, not as usable archive readers. PPC-only XPK compressors are not planned. The README gives no license name for the project itself beyond the claim of BSD-style licensing, and it says the BZIP2 randomization tables carry the bzip2 license. The homepage was reachable.
quotes: Decompression routines for long-dead file formats
Provide a clean, modern implementation of the algorithms
The code is no good if it does not work properly and the old code have a lot of corner cases.
I'm slowly adding new stuff. If your favorite is not listed contact me and maybe I can add it.
fetch_log: https://github.com/temisu/ancient - worked, returned the README. Not thin, so I did not follow further links.

judge.reason: A modern, tested decompressor for dozens of obscure Amiga and Atari formats opens a compelling window into old binary formats and digital preservation.

entry.title: ancient
entry.tldr: A command-line decompressor for dead Amiga and Atari compression formats like ByteKiller, PowerPacker and Pack-Ice, rewritten cleanly and tested on about 10,000 real files.
entry.deeper_look:
Ancient is a C++ library with a small command-line tool on top. You give it a file packed by one of dozens of old formats, mostly from Amiga and Atari machines in the 1980s and 1990s, and it detects the format in most cases and writes out the decompressed data. The list includes ByteKiller, Pack-Ice, PowerPacker, StoneCracker, DMS and XPK wrappers, plus Unix compress/pack, gzip and bzip2.

The reason it exists is that many of these algorithms can still be found, but the originals were written for the machines they ran on. Some ports are incomplete or poor, and some are direct translations of M68K assembly. Licensing is often unclear or missing. The author's answer is clean modern implementations under a BSD-style license, tested against a cache of roughly 10k real files. In the author's words: "The code is no good if it does not work properly and the old code have a lot of corner cases."

The idea underneath is that a compression format is a small, complete piece of reverse engineering. Each one is a tight bit of design shaped by the memory and CPU limits of its machine. Detection is not always reliable, because the old formats had weaknesses, which shows how little these files said about themselves. Some formats, such as DMS and PowerPacker PX20, have weak password protection that the code can bypass. The project says it does not do real cryptography.

It does not handle archives or self-extracting executables. Zip and LZH exist only as backends, not as usable archive readers.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the tool's usage, which is the place to start since the README shows no example commands.

entry.whats_unique: It covers a large number of obscure Amiga and Atari formats in one tool, many of which exist nowhere else as clean modern code. It was also rewritten under BSD-style terms to settle the unclear licensing of the originals.
entry.caveats: The README has no build or usage instructions, detection is unreliable for some formats, several formats are marked 'verification missing', and archives and self-extracting executables are not supported.
